paper_title: Foresight Forcing: Learning Spatial Foresight for Robotic Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing ($\mathcal{F}^{2}$), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, $\mathcal{F}^{2}$ achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Robotic manipulation has progressed from task-specific systems designed for controlled environments towards generalist policies that operate across diverse objects, instructions, and settings. general-purpose robot must interpret task instructions, perceive objects in its surroundings, and execute precise actions under varying conditions. Recent advances in large-scale robot learning and pretrained vision-language models have enabled Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions [3, 4, 14, 15, 48]. However, action labels do not directly supervise the visual outcomes of those actions. To incorporate this information into policy learning, World Action Models (WAMs) build on visual generative models and couple action learning with world modeling objectives [2, 6, 45, 47]. The resulting visual prediction task provides an additional training signal alongside action supervision and enables robot policies to benefit from pretrained generative representations. Most WAMs learn how scene evolves by predicting future RGB observations or visual latents. These objectives encode task-relevant spatial relationships alongside object appearance, background, and viewpoint, leaving the geometric transitions that matter for control implicit. Geometry Forcing shows that pretrained 3D features can improve the geometric consistency of video generation [40], and geometry-aware WAMs have explored geometric supervision for manipulation [19, 24, 46]. For robot control, the 3D changes needed to advance the task provide natural target for this supervision. Placing an object requires changing its pose relative to target, while opening drawer requires changing the configuration of an articulated object. Modeling such transitions gives the policy way to anticipate how the scene needs to change when generating actions. Therefore, we introduce Foresight Forcing (F 2), WAM that fuses correspondence-aligned transitions in 3D geometry feature space of foundation models into spatial transition queries for action generation, rather than directly predicting explicit 3D motions (Figure 1). During training, frozen VGGT teacher [32] extracts patch features from an aligned observation pair, and their temporal differences serve as dense targets for the queries. shared updater progressively refines the queries after each double block of the visual backbone using information from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state. We supervise the queries to match the direction and scale of the teacher targets and feed the refined queries directly to the action expert. At inference, the policy predicts the queries from its current inputs without access to future observations or the teacher. We evaluate 2 on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks to assess manipulation performance, robustness, and inference eﬀiciency. 2 achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real robot. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Transition-centric geometric supervision. We introduce correspondence-aligned 3D teacher feature differences as supervision for spatial transition learning for action generation in World Action Model. Teacher-guided spatial transition learning for action generation. We introduce dedicated latent queries that shared updater progressively refines across the visual backbone. During training, we align the refined queries with the frozen 3D teacher targets in direction and scale. The queries directly condition the action expert. Manipulation performance and robustness. Evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, with state-of-the-art average success rates on RoboTwin 2.0 Full and Clean-to-Random. On six real-world tasks, 2 achieves mean task score of 85.8%, exceeding ImageWAM and π0.5 by 15.6 and 2.3 percentage points, respectively.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: World Action Models. World Action Models (WAMs) jointly learn action generation and future visual prediction through autoregressive video-action modeling, shared latent representations, compact future conditions, or image-based prediction [2, 6, 18, 30, 45, 47]. Visual prediction provides supervision for control, even when future images are not generated during execution. Building on ImageWAM, we study complementary signal: the spatial transition between current and future observations. 2 Figure 2 2 architecture. frozen VGGT provides feature transition targets on the student grid for spatial queries Insets show the shared updater and spatial query layout. VGGT and future that condition the Action Expert. observations are used only during training. 3D Representations for Visual Generation. Feed-forward 3D models recover spatial structure and dense features from images. DUSt3R and MASt3R establish pairwise geometry and correspondences [16, 36]; subsequent models extend inference to multiple views and image streams [20, 3234, 39, 42]. REPA aligns diffusion representations with pretrained visual features [44], while geometric features guide consistent video generation and image editing [23, 25, 40]. We use frozen VGGT to encode paired observations and supervise the policy with correspondence-aligned differences between its current and future features. Geometry in Action Learning. Existing action models incorporate geometry either as an observation or predicted spatial representation, or as supervision for learned features. The former includes geometric inputs, point flow, trajectories, future pointmaps, and spatially structured actions [9, 11, 12, 26, 35, 41, 46]. The latter uses geometric objectives or distilled priors to shape policy representations [17, 19, 24]. Foresight Forcing instead supervises dedicated spatial queries with correspondence-aligned temporal differences in 3D teacher features. The queries are predicted from current inputs and directly condition the action expert.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Building on this framework, 2 introduces spatial transition queries that encode task-relevant geometric changes over the action horizon. During training, frozen 3D teacher supplies feature differences between aligned current and future observations as dense targets. The queries condition action generation alongside current visual features; neither future observations nor the teacher is required at deployment (Figure 2). We formulate the task in Sec. 3.1, construct the geometric transition target in Sec. 3.2, explain how the queries learn from it in Sec. 3.3, and detail training and deployment in Sec. 3.4.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate manipulation performance, robustness to distribution shifts, the contributions of individual components, real-world applicability, and inference cost.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate 2 on LIBERO [22], LIBERO-Plus [10], RoboTwin 2.0 [8], and real-world manipulation tasks. LIBERO is single-arm simulation benchmark; we evaluate its Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites, each containing 10 tasks. LIBERO-Plus tests robustness across seven perturbation dimensions: object layout, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language instruction, lighting, background, and observation noise. RoboTwin 2.0 comprises 50 dual-arm manipulation tasks in simulated tabletop scenes, including object placement, stacking, tool use, and articulated-object interaction. We evaluate both its Full and Clean-to-Random settings under clean and randomized scenes. For real-world evaluation, we compare three methods on six manipulation tasks. 5 Table 1 LIBERO benchmark. sections.title: 4.2 In-Distribution Performance
sections.content: We first examine whether 2 maintains strong standard manipulation performance when the evaluation follows the training distribution. LIBERO. Table 1 reports success on the four standard suites. Each suite contains 10 tasks, and we evaluate each task over 50 trials. 2 achieves an average success rate of 98.5%, compared with 98.4% for ImageWAM and matching the leading methods at the reported precision. As these methods approach the success-rate ceiling, standard LIBERO offers limited headroom for distinguishing their performance. In the RoboTwin 2.0 Full setting, 2 achieves the highest clean, randomized, and average RoboTwin 2.0. success rates in Table 2, without robot-policy pretraining. It reaches 94.90% and 95.12% in the clean and randomized settings, respectively, improving over ImageWAM by 1.70 and 1.56 percentage points. Its average success is 95.01%, compared with 94.55% for Flex-π. The gains over ImageWAM in both settings suggest that spatial transition supervision benefits manipulation across the evaluated scene conditions. Per-task results are reported in Appendix B.

sections.title: 4.4 Ablation and Mechanism Analysis
sections.content: We conduct ablation studies on LIBERO-Plus to examine the supervision and design of spatial transition queries. All variants use the same training data as the 2 baseline and are trained for 10 epochs. Figure 3 summarizes the results, which we discuss through three questions. Does supervising geometric transitions improve the queries? We first examine whether the queries benefit from teacher target. In the supervision-target comparison in Figure 3, feature-delta supervision improves success from 82.3% without distillation to 84.5%, indicating contribution beyond the additional query tokens. We then compare what the teacher supplies: the aligned feature difference outperforms both currentand future-feature targets, which reach 83.2% and 81.2%, respectively. Unlike an individual-frame target, the feature difference relates the paired observations and supervises how their teacher representations 7 Figure 3 Ablation study on LIBERO-Plus. Each group varies one factor while retaining the other default settings; all variants are trained for 10 epochs. change; however, the target remains feature-space representation rather than direct measurement of 3D motion. How does target construction affect performance? We next examine the effect of the teacher representation used to construct the feature-difference target. DINOv3 [27], VGGT, and π3 [39] yield 83.4%, 84.5%, and 82.9%, respectively. Among the tested teachers, VGGT achieves the strongest performance. Its improvement over DINOv3 suggests that geometry-oriented teacher features can provide useful spatial supervision for manipulation, while the result with π3 shows that the choice of geometric teacher also matters. How do query design and action conditioning affect performance? Finally, we examine how the transition signal is represented and used for action generation. The frame-matched budget of = 392 queries (LIBEROs 1428 two-view token grid) performs best among the tested sizes, while both 200 and 512 queries perform worse, showing that simply increasing the budget does not guarantee improvement. This comparison varies the query budget and does not isolate the effect of spatial correspondence from other changes in the representation. With the query grid in place, removing the shared updater while retaining native masked attention (leaving self-attention-only, without access to current visual or instruction tokens) reduces success from 84.5% to 81.7%, supporting the complete updater design for integrating current visual and conditioning states. sections.title: 4.5 Real-World Evaluation
sections.content: We evaluate physical manipulation on six tasks: cup stacking, towel folding, egg transfer, breakfast preparation, tool stowing, and size sorting. We compare π0.5 [3], ImageWAM [47], and 2, each jointly trained on the six tasks. Table 5 summarizes the comparison over 15 trials per task, and Figure 6 illustrates the tasks; demonstration statistics and detailed success criteria are provided in Appendix C. Success criteria. Cup stacking, towel folding, egg transfer, and breakfast preparation require full-task completion. Tool stowing and size sorting use item-level success rates. Each tool-stowing trial contains four tools, while each size-sorting trial contains 15 blocks and is scored by the fraction correctly sorted. 2 achieves an average score of 85.8%, compared with 83.5% for π0.5 and 70.2% for ImageWAM. Whereas ImageWAM reports strong real-world performance on its original suite [47], its lower scores here reflect differences in task suites, demonstrations, and evaluation protocols. In particular, several of our tasks require consecutive manipulation steps, during which the policy must respond to changing object configurations. The learned transition representation may provide useful spatial information for these tasks. Although 2 is trained without robot pretraining, its results are competitive with the pretrained π0.5 on several tasks. sections.title: 4.6 Inference Efficiency
sections.content: We assess the inference cost of spatial transition conditioning in Table 6. Under the same measurement settings, 2 takes 195.01 2.99 ms per 16-action chunk, compared with 187.41 4.80 ms for ImageWAM. This modest 4.1% increase accompanies the manipulation improvements reported above. The small overhead indicates that the additional query pathway largely preserves the runtime eﬀiciency of the underlying WAM. To improve inference speed for real-world deployment, we apply CUDA Graph optimization to both methods. The optimized ImageWAM and 2 achieve 80.20 3.74 ms and 99.53 3.26 ms per chunk, respectively. For 2, this reduces the inference latency by approximately 49%, supporting more responsive action generation during real-world execution.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: F 2 learns spatial transition queries from correspondence-aligned changes in pretrained 3D features. These queries provide the Action Expert with representation of anticipated spatial change, connecting geometric supervision during training to action generation from current observations. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and six real-world tasks show strong manipulation performance and improved robustness. Together, the results suggest that supervising how scene changes in 3D feature space is useful complement to future-image prediction in world action models. Studying how spatial transition learning generalizes across broader tasks, embodiments, and environments is an important direction for future research.

A.1 Soft Spatial Alignment For each view v, we estimate dense backward optical flow (target-to-reference Farnebäck flow) from the future observation t+H to the current observation , and warp the current image onto the future-image grid: eI (x) = (x + v(x)) , (10) where indexes pixel on the future grid. binary validity map records whether each warped coordinate falls inside the current image bounds and is average-pooled to obtain patch-level validity weights mp [0, 1]. Alignment is applied prior to frozen VGGT feature extraction. On LIBERO-Plus, enabling soft spatial alignment improves overall success from 81.9% to 84.5% (+2.6 percentage points; Table 7). Devices 15 1 8 NVIDIA H200 24 1 32 NVIDIA H200 8 1 128 T-Head PPU-ZW810E A.3 Teacher and Spatial Layout The frozen VGGT aggregator outputs patch features of channel width = 2048. Camera and register tokens are stripped prior to bilinear interpolation onto each cameras region in the student token grid. Our layout supports horizontal and vertical multi-view concatenations as well as the RoboTwin three-view mosaic (a top head view above two side-by-side wrist views). Image crops, teacher features, flow-validity masks (Sec. A.1), and transition queries share identical spatial bounding boxes within the mosaic. Feature subtraction and geometry-loss reductions are computed in FP32 to preserve small feature differences across large teacher activations. A.4 Distillation Details The spatial projector Pθ maps the transition query grid from width to the teacher feature width via two 3 3 convolutional layers (each followed by SiLU activation) and 1 1 output convolution. The scale head Sθ is two-layer MLP with an intermediate SiLU activation. Omitting the batch index for clarity, patch sums and means are computed per training example and subsequently averaged over the batch. The patch weights used in Sec. 3.3 are defined as " wp = mp η + (1 η) N 1 y,p2 r=1 y,r2 + ϵ # , (11) where mp [0, 1] is the pooled flow-validity mask, η balances uniform and magnitude-weighted supervision, ϵ is small constant for numerical stability, and the denominator averages over all student-grid locations across views. All teacher-derived weights and norm targets are detached from backpropagation. The geometry warm-up schedule follows ρ(k) = ρ0 + (1 ρ0) min(k/Kw, 1), where is the optimization step, ρ0 is the initial multiplier, and Kw = 0.05 Ttotal is the warm-up horizon relative to the total number of optimization steps Ttotal. A.5 Learned Transition Visualization Feature-change maps. For Figure 4(a), we compute the channel-wise ℓ2 norm of the aligned VGGT feature difference alongside the corresponding prediction from the trained geometry head. External-camera maps are bilinearly upsampled from the 14 14 patch grid and rendered under shared color scale and response threshold to emphasize salient regions. Both maps are overlaid on an equal blend of the current and observed-future frames separated by = 16 steps. Future frames are used only to compute the teacher target and visualization background; student queries are predicted solely from the current observation and language instruction. Future-point visualization. For Figure 4(b), we freeze the trained policy and fit lightweight two-layer MLP probe to automatically tracked point correspondences. Taking local and pooled features together with the current query coordinates as input, the probe predicts 2D image-space displacements and is used strictly for post-hoc visualization. Query points are sampled within visible object regions in the current frame, and CoTracker3 [13] tracks them across observed video clips as well as current/ImageWAM-generated image pairs. We retain tracks that remain visible within image bounds and satisfy 2-pixel forwardbackward cycle consistency check. Observed future frames are withheld from both probe prediction and generated-image localization. The plate example is drawn from the 16 held-out probe test split, whereas the mug and book examples come from its training split; CoTracker3 trajectories serve as estimated correspondence references. A.6 Data Augmentation During training, we apply synchronized image augmentations across frames within each camera view, including resized cropping, rotation, color jitter, gamma adjustment, and Gaussian noise. Under the RoboTwin Clean-to-Random setting, following PatchWAM [37], we additionally apply stronger appearance augmentations comprising photometric jitter, Gaussian blur, AdaIN-style feature-statistic perturbation, and Fourier amplitude modulation. Spatial transformations are shared between student and teacher inputs so geometric correspondence is preserved, whereas appearance augmentations are applied solely to the student inputs. A.7 TrainingInference Visibility Figure 7 illustrates the native MoT attention masks used during training and inference. Within the native MoT blocks, transition queries perform self-attention only, preventing any leakage from future-image tokens during training; they instead aggregate current visual and conditioning features through the shared updater Uθ using identical currentonly context at both training and test time. At inference, future-image tokens are absent and the Action Expert attends jointly to current visual states Hcur and transition queries Z. Figure 7 Attention visibility. Native MoT attention masks during training (left) and inference (right), with query rows and key/value columns. The conditioning stream Hℓ combines language instructions and encoded proprioceptive state, and hatched cells denote rows whose query tokens are noisy (Hfuture and A). For the action stream A, the half-filled Hcur cell indicates stochastic reference access (q = 0.5) during training, which becomes full visibility at inference when future tokens are absent. Outside this mask, the shared updater in Figure 2 supplies with current visual and conditioning features. RoboTwin 2.0 Evaluation Details B.1 Per-Task Results Tables 14 and 15 (placed at the end of the appendix) report per-task success rates for all 50 tasks in the RoboTwin 2.0 Full and Clean-to-Random benchmarks summarized in Tables 2 and 4, respectively. For 2, every task is evaluated over 100 episodes under both clean and randomized conditions; baseline numbers in the Full table follow the ImageWAM codebase. B.2 Additional Clean-to-Random Experiments All runs start from the InternData-A1-pretrained ImageWAM model and use the same clean RoboTwin demonstrations and 50-task C2R benchmark. The ImageWAM baseline is trained for 50 epochs without additional appearance augmentation and obtains 70.35% average success. Our main result trains 2 for the same 50-epoch stage, followed by 20 additional epochs with additional augmentation, reaching 77.45%. All variants use the same evaluation protocol, with 100 episodes per task under both clean and randomized conditions. ImageWAM with additional augmentation. Continuing the 50-epoch ImageWAM baseline for 20 more epochs with additional augmentation yields 84.18% on clean scenes, 67.82% on randomized scenes, and 76.00% on average. 17 2 without additional augmentation. Continuing the same 50-epoch ImageWAM baseline for 20 more epochs with 2 but without additional augmentation yields 82.32%, 60.04%, and 71.18% on clean, randomized, and average success, respectively. Table 12 summarizes the training variants and results. Additional augmentation improves the ImageWAM baseline from 70.35% to 76.00%, while 2 further improves the augmented result to 77.45%. Without augmentation, 2 reaches 71.18%, exceeding the ImageWAM baseline. The 0.83-point improvement over ImageWAM without additional augmentation supports the benefit of introducing transition supervision. Under the augmented schedule, 2 also outperforms ImageWAM by 1.45 points, providing further evidence of its contribution. These results support the value of transition supervision both with and without additional augmentation. Table 12 RoboTwin Clean-to-Random training controls. The robot unstacks nested pile of cups into horizontal row and then stacks them into pyramid. trial succeeds if the entire sequence finishes within the time limit. Minor execution errors (e.g., missed grasps, tipped cups, or overlapping placements) are permitted if the policy autonomously recovers and completes the pyramid within the allotted time; otherwise, the trial fails. Towel folding. The robot folds flat towel in half, folds it in half second time, and presses the folded cloth flat. trial succeeds only if all three steps are completed cleanly; failure at any stage counts as failed trial. Egg transfer. The robot transfers eggs from source carton into designated slots in destination tray. trial succeeds when all eggs are properly seated in the tray; rolling eggs or visibly misplaced placements count as failure. 18 Breakfast preparation. The robot sequentially places slice of bread, fried egg, second slice of bread, banana, and carrot onto plate. trial succeeds if the full assembly completes within the time limit, including autonomous recovery from intermediate mistakes; any incomplete sequence counts as failure. Tool stowing. Each trial presents four articulated tools to be placed into fitted organizer slots in toolbox. We score the fraction of tools stowed successfully; if tool fails, it is marked as failure and an operator places it so the policy can proceed to the remaining tools. The reported score is the total number of stowed tools divided by 60 across 15 trials. Size sorting. Each trial contains 15 blocks to be sorted by size into large box and small box. We report the mean fraction of correctly sorted blocks across 15 trials. block counts as failure if the robot fails to grasp it, selects the wrong box, or drops it outside the target box.

sections.title: D Attention Analysis
sections.content: We apply an identical diagnostic procedure to ImageWAM and 2 on randomized RoboTwin observations (Figure 5), holding the current RGB inputs, proprioceptive state, instruction, and sampling seed fixed within each pair to compare the two methods under matched inputs. For Figure 5, we adapt attention rollout [1] with gradient-weighted attention propagation [7], combining head-averaged positive attentiongradient products with additive residual transport across the image backbone, shared query updater, and Action Expert. Attribution targets the first actions left-gripper component at the final denoising step with earlier action latents held fixed. Routes are grouped by their entry edge into the action stream and normalized over all three camera views (only the head view is displayed). ImageWAM Evaluation on LIBERO-Plus The ImageWAM baseline in Table 3 reflects our evaluation of the oﬀicially released FLUX.2 [klein] 4B checkpoint under the exact same protocol as 2, yielding an overall success rate of 81.6% (used in Sec. 4.3) rather than the 83.1% originally reported in [47]. As clarified by the ImageWAM authors in repository Issue #3,1 the originally reported 4B figure was evaluated on 15% subset using sampling seed 42, and the released evaluation script defaulted to text context length of 128 whereas the 4B checkpoint was trained with 512.
